title: SEBI Chief Tells Mutual Fund Industry to Measure Success by Investor Outcomes, Not AUM
excerpt: At AMFIs 31st Foundation Day, Chairman Pandey set a target of doubling Indias mutual fund investor base to 12 crore and urged a shift from asset accumulation to investor returns.
body:
• SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey urged the mutual fund industry to measure success by investor outcomes rather than AUM growth, folio counts, or scheme numbers.
  • India's mutual fund AUM has grown from ₹15 lakh crore to ₹86 lakh crore over the past decade, a compound annual growth rate of 19%.
  • Pandey set an ambitious target of doubling India's mutual fund investor base from 6 crore to 12 crore over the coming years.
  • Women now account for 34% of individual investor AUM, and 22% of Indian households indicated they intend to enter capital markets within 12 months.

Securities and Exchange Board of India Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey delivered a pointed message to India's mutual fund industry on Friday: stop measuring success by the size of your assets and start measuring it by what investors actually earn.

Speaking at the Association of Mutual Funds in India's 31st Foundation Day in Mumbai, Pandey acknowledged the industry's rapid growth but challenged fund houses to shift their focus from scale to substance.

A Decade of Growth, A Question of Depth

The numbers tell a story of remarkable expansion. India's mutual fund assets under management have surged from approximately ₹15 lakh crore in July 2016 to about ₹86 lakh crore in July 2026, registering a compound annual growth rate of around 19%. Monthly systematic investment plan contributions now stand at roughly ₹32,000 crore, and the country has more than 14 crore unique capital market investors.

Yet Pandey cautioned against complacency. "Success cannot be measured only by AUM, number of folios or schemes; it must ultimately be measured by investor outcomes," he said.

"Success cannot be measured only by AUM, number of folios or schemes; it must ultimately be measured by investor outcomes."

— Tuhin Kanta Pandey, Chairman, SEBI

The gap between awareness and action remains significant. A SEBI Investors Survey conducted in 2025 found that while more than half of respondents were aware of mutual funds or ETFs, only 6.7% of Indian households actually invested in them.

The 12-Crore Target

Pandey set an ambitious goal: doubling the number of unique mutual fund investors from the current 6 crore to approximately 12 crore over the next few years. He urged the industry to work backwards from this objective, identifying the distribution networks, investor awareness campaigns, and product innovations needed to reach the target.

The push extends to underrepresented demographics and geographies. While mutual funds have expanded their reach to almost every pin code in India, Pandey said investor education must become more multilingual, multi-agency, and multimedia. He specifically highlighted women's growing participation, noting that women now account for 34% of individual investor AUM.

AMFI's Outreach Expansion

AMFI has responded with a slate of new outreach initiatives. The industry body has launched investor awareness programmes in states including Odisha, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, and Meghalaya, supplemented by regional-language campaigns. Outreach now extends to non-traditional audiences including gig workers and self-help groups.

SEBI has also launched Project 'Jagrook', a national initiative focused on multilingual media outreach and a unified effort by the regulator and its securities market partners to strengthen investor education across the country.

The regulator's efforts align with broader market data showing latent demand. The SEBI Investors Survey 2025 found that 22% of Indian households intended to enter the capital markets within the following 12 months — a significant pool of potential investors that the industry has yet to convert.

What's Next

The mutual fund industry's next chapter will be defined by its ability to translate scale into quality returns for a broader investor base. With Pandey explicitly tying regulatory goodwill to investor outcomes rather than asset accumulation, fund houses face pressure to demonstrate that their products deliver genuine wealth creation — particularly for the millions of first-time SIP investors who have entered the market in recent years.
